content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a modeling approach to estimate the causal effects of multiple treatments over a sequence of time. This is an ambitious line of research that incorporates counterfactual inference, domain adversarial training and, contrastive learning to handle the various complexities of the problem setting. The proposed method TCFimt is applied to two distinct domains, gaming and healthcare, to demonstrate it's general utility and is compared to a large variety of approaches as baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I wish that I had a better grasp of the proposed contributions so I would be able to list a longer list of the strengths of this paper. Unfortunately the writing and construction of this paper is very poor which severely limited my ability to get a better sense of what the authors have done and how to fully evaluate the proposed TCFimt method. As such my "Strengths" section here is shorter in comparison to the "Weaknesses" section. 

### Strengths

This is a very difficult problem and I appreciate that the authors have not let that difficulty stop them from proposing a solution that seems reasonable and valid from a conceptual basis. The use of domain adversarial training to improve the representation learning of the sequence of observations, leading hopefully to less biased predictions of the outcomes under different interventions, is a great inclusion within the multitude of components used to construct TCFimt.

The figures are mostly well constructed and attempt to illustrate complex concepts. I felt that Figure 2 especially helped improve my understanding of Section 3. 

### Weaknesses

This paper introduces a very complex method to address a difficult problem. This isn't a deal breaker necessarily but it requires a very clear and simple justification as well as adequate context to communicate the necessity of all of the piece parts. I found the paper very difficult to read and understand even on the second and third time. The authors attempted to use figures and clear notation to aid in the process but there was far too much contextual information that was omitted from the paper entirely or relegated to the appendix with very vague references in the main body of the paper. Also the figures are not adequately captioned and there is fairly little discussion in the paper that aligns with the specific details that are supposed to be illustrated in the figures. For all of these issues I will list specific questions for each below:

- There is a good deal of domain-specific terminology that could be better explained or even clarified. Examples of this are "mega-event", "mixed intervention", "treatment effect", "temporal bias", "selection bias", "corruption function", "pseudo-counterfactual", etc. Some of these are relatively familiar but aren't put into adequate context. Without describing or giving a clear example of what these things are and why they're important to keep in consideration, the paper suffers from the very outset. 
- There is a shocking lack of citation throughout the paper. The motivations and framing of the paper, as a result, come across as vague and speculative. There is no adequate framing of why multiple treatment effect estimation has been ignored and what attempts there have been to address it. As such, I cannot adequately assess the significance of this paper.
-  What's the difference between a "pseudo-counterfactual" and "counterfactual". I would suspect that they're the same thing... No need to overcomplicate the semantics of the method...
- The concepts underlying the proposed contributions are not introduced anywhere in the introduction. Primarily the notion of "interventional effect decoupling" and "causal interaction issue" are not defined previously (or elsewhere in the paper).
- What is the "unconfoundedness assumption"? Is this **Assumption 1** --> There needs to be a plain language description of what this assumption means practically.
- There is fairly little explained how the time varying variables $X_t$ interact with the features of a treatment $V_t$. Also, do the specific $V_t$ for each treatment $A_k$ vary in time? If not, why are they indexed with time? 
- Are the outcomes temporally varying? Or is the outcome $Y_t$ a single prediction quantity for each individual sequence? It's not clear how the observations $X$, interventions $A$ and outcomes $Y$ are related. Is there a functional relationship or is $Y_t$ a subset of the time series $X_{t-1}$ that is being forecast? This is a critical omission in the description and set-up of the paper.
- The paper really starts to "fall apart" in Section 3. There is so much information and conceptual framing that is hurried and the connections between the different concepts are not clearly laid out. It's unclear what the use of the joint factual and counterfactual representations are (looking at Figures 3 and 4, it's unclear why there's a stacked input to the RNN modules but then on the right of the figure you only use the counterfactual representation? I found Figure 4 to be especially confusing. There's not an adequate description of what's going on in the main body of the text and the caption is unhelpful. The gradient lines don't point anywhere. Ultimately the disconnect between the various concepts and structures in Section 3 lead me to believe that this isn't a complete paper.
- I cannot trust the setting of the experiments without any introduction, context, or justification for the baselines used. There is no information about what the different domains are and why they are valid for testing the TCFimt method.
- With all of the complexities of the proposed TCFimt method. It's surprising that the authors don't perform model ablations to demonstrate that all of the piece parts are necessary and what the gains are for including them each in the overall method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**: Very poor (see above)

**Quality**: 
 - Conceptual framing: Good
 - Writing: Very poor

**Novelty**: Good
 - While the various building blocks used to develop TCFimt are not new, their use for a difficult and relatively unaddressed major challenge in real-world causal effect estimation is notable and welcome. This novelty is somewhat hard to firmly assess however as the authors have included surprisingly little motivating context for their work and include zero framing from related literature throughout the main body of the paper.

**Reproducibility**: Poor
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors address a challenging problem and should be commended, however the solution they have presented is exceptionally complex and has a large number of components drawn from very distinct research areas. This complexity might be warranted but is very difficult to communicate in a cohesive manner. Unfortunately this paper severely suffers in terms of its clarity of each component and how they all fit together. It's apparent that the authors recognized this difficulty and tried their best to provide figures and clear notation but it didn't all come together very well. I believe that the paper requires a substantial revision to provide a more understandable and coherent demonstration of the proposed TCFimt. The material seems to all be in place but there are many errors and unclear or vague references to concepts/ideas that are undiscussed in the paper and are otherwise not cited. As the paper is currently written, despite the importance of the problem setting and the seemingly promising results, I cannot recommend its publication. In its current state this paper would not be of much use to the research community.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the problem of estimating the causal effects of multiple treatments in the temporal setting. The authors propose using a corruption function to augment the dataset by generating pseudo-counterfactual data of multiple treatments; then the proposed method uses adversarial training to handle the time-varying bias and contrastive learning to improve the prediction of effects under mixed interventions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- the paper tackles a highly relevant and understudied problem in the causal inference literature. 

Weaknesses:
- The papers lists several reasons why "Existing causal inference techniques under the longitudinal setting such as Recurrent Marginal Structural Networks (RMSN, Lim et al., 2018) and Counterfactual Recurrent Network (CRN, Bica et al., 2020) cannot be applied to conduct causal inference of multiple treatments in temporal data.”; however, I believe these are flawed as these methods were also designed to handle the case of only having access to the factual outcomes (which is always the case in causal inference) and to handle the selection bias present in observational datasets. Moreover, RMSN can be used to handle multiple treatments (i.e. treatment combinations) in the temporal setting. 
- Assumption 2. (causal interactions) introduced by the paper is not a standard assumption in the literature and it seems to be a strong assumption. Moreover, there is no reference to other works making this assumption. In this situation, I believe that the authors need to provide a more thorough description of why it’s needed and its implications.
- Several claims in the paper are misleading. For instance, the paper mentions that "temporal causal inference methods focus on single treatment regimen, ignoring realistic situations of multiple treatment assignments.” - this is not the case as both Marginal Structural Models (Robins et al., 2000) and Recurrent Marginal Structural Networks (Lim et al., 2018 ) can handle the case of multiple treatment assignments.
- I believe that the current description of the  PSEUDO-COUNTERFACTUALS GENERATION in Section 3.1 is insufficient to properly understand the proposed approach. In particular, it is unclear how corrupting the treatments and the interventional features helps us with obtaining outcomes under other treatment options. 
- The proposed method does adversarial balancing for each different treatment individually, thus needing K classifiers of the treatment. However, it is unclear how this results in a balanced representation against several different treatment options (e.g. $P(\Phi(H_t) | A_{t, 1} = 0, A_{t, 2}= 1, A_{t, 3}=0) = P(\Phi(H_t) | A_{t, 1} = 1, A_{t, 2} = 1, A_{t, 3}=1)$, which is what is needed in this case of multiple treatments.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The adversarial training proposed that involves simultaneously maximizing the error of the treatment classification task and minimizing the error of the outcomes prediction task has already been proposed in CRN; the paper uses the same approach without giving any references to CRN in the introduction and description of the method, which is misleading. Moreover, the encoder-decoder framework used is very similar to the one in CRN and RMSN. This reduces the novelty of the proposed approach. 
- The paper mentions selection bias and time-varying bias as two separate problems, but these are the same issues in the temporal causal inference setting. 
- Overall, I think the paper needs more references to support the claims made and to provide a more accurate acknowledgement of existing work. For instance, the paper mentions that "Most existing methods estimate individual treatment effects in static setting without considering the time-varying confounders.” without giving any reference to what these existing methods are. Moreover, the proof in appendix C.2 is very similar to the proof in appendix D in CRN, but the authors do not provide any reference to existing work making the same proof. 
- I believe that the Experiments section needs to contain more details about the datasets used for evaluation. Moreover, for the Games dataset, it is not clear how the counterfactuals are obtained and how any temporal covariates are defined (this is also unclear after looking at the appendix)
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper addresses an important and understudied problem, I think the issues mentioned above need to be addressed before the paper is ready for publication. Moreover, I think the paper would significantly benefit from more clarity when describing the problem set-up they are aiming to solve and a more accurate description of the differences with related work.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of temporal counterfactual prediction problem with time-varying bias and multiple treatment interventions. The authors adopt an adversarial module to address time-varying bias and a contrastive module to separate mixed treatment effects. Experiments are conducted on two datasets for performance evaluation with state-of-the-art methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The studied problem is meaningful and challenging in many real scenarios. 

Weaknesses:
1. Assumption 2 (causal interactions) is not well-illustrated. 
	a. There is no discussion of whether this assumption is valid in real-world observational data. 
	b. There is no discussion of whether this assumption is still correct with the increasing number of available treatment options (as the method is mainly designed for multi-treatment settings). The interaction pattern will definitely become more and more complex among different treatments thus this simple additive equation may not characterize such complex interaction. 
	c. It is not clear how to evaluate the estimated causal interaction in the experiment. 

2. The pseudo-counterfactuals generation process is unclear. 
	a. More details of the counterfactual generation and how it can be applied to real-world datasets are required. 
	b. The motivation for using the corruption function generation method instead of other existing generation methods (e.g., generative adversarial nets-based counterfactual generation method [Yoon et al., 2018]) is not illustrated. Why this corruption function is superior to the existing work in this temporal multi-treatment setting? Any empirical experiments to show the performance comparison among the corruption function and SOTA?

3. The experiments are not solid and comprehensive to well demonstrate the model performance in counterfactual prediction under time-varying and mixed treatment effects scenarios. 
	a. The available number of treatment options is limited in both datasets. In Games, only 2 and 3 treatment options are available according to Table 3. In Tumor, only 3 treatment options actually are available and there is only one possible treatment combination: combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Experiments on such a simple dataset are not comprehensive and solid to demonstrate the model performance and further support the claims that "experiments on real-world data ... validate the effectiveness of our methods". 
	b. All the baselines including the ablation of the proposed method should be compared in both two datasets. 
	c. The variability of the main results (i.e., standard deviations or confidence intervals of multiple runs, etc.) should be provided in Table 1 and Table 2. 	
	d. There are some existing works (e.g., Parbhoo et al., 2021) that study the counterfactual prediction in the combination treatment setting, which are very related and should be considered for comparison. 
	e. The search range and optimal values for hyperparameters lambda_1 and lambda_2 in Equation (17) should be provided. 

4. It is unclear what is the interventional feature in real-world datasets. 

References
Yoon, Jinsung, James Jordon, and Mihaela Van Der Schaar. "GANITE: Estimation of individualized treatment effects using generative adversarial nets." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.
Parbhoo, Sonali, Stefan Bauer, and Patrick Schwab. "Ncore: Neural counterfactual representation learning for combinations of treatments." arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.11175 (2021).

4. The code/data is not provided for review.
